source_text: Haud sane impugnavero eos qui autumant Adam, si dicto audiens exstitisset, ad immortalitatem potuisse pro remuneratione transferri. Enoch quippe et Eliam translatos legimus, ne viderent mortem. Verum aliud sunt instituta naturae, aliud praemia obedientiae. Non est enim tanti unius meritum, ut universa quae naturaliter sunt instituta perturbet. Exercuisset se igitur in reliquis innata mortalitas, etiamsi primus ille in aeternitatem a diuturnitate migrasset. Non inficiabili coniectura, sed certo res tenetur exemplo, siquidem Enoch filii, immortalitate parentis non potuerunt asseri a conditione moriendi. Nec illud forte putetur occurrere, quoniam si non peccatores, iusti tamen omnes ad immortalitatem sine intercessu corporalis dissipationis evaderent: siquidem Abel iustorum primus, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, et omnia sanctorum agmina, tam in Novo quam in Vetere Testamento, et meritum suum virtutibus, et naturam morte docuerunt. Rem in absoluto positam Christi quoque confirmavit auctoritas. Nam cum ei Sadducaei quaestionem exemplo septinubae mulieris intulissent, rogantes, si corporum excitatio crederetur, a quo marito esset potissimum vindicanda, respondit: Erratis, nescientes Scripturas, neque Dei virtutem; in resurrectione enim neque nubent, neque uxores accipient; neque enim morientur [n183] . Conscius operis sui, propter quid coniugia instituisset expressit, videlicet ut damna mortis fetura suppleret; statim autem cessatum ire munificam fecunditatem, cum mors avara cessaverit. Si ergo, Christo teste qui condidit, fertilitas ob hoc creata est, ut cum fragilitate confligeret, et haec conditio nuptiarum ante peccatum ordinata est; apparet quoque mortalitatem non ad praevaricationem spectare, sed ad naturam ad quam spectare leguntur et nuptiae. Illa ergo lex quae promulgata est, id est: Quacumque die ex interdicto ederis, morte morieris; poenalis mors intellegitur, non corporalis; peccatis, non seminibus imminens; quam non incurrit nisi praevaricatio, non evadit nisi emendatio. Die autem peccati quod dicitur inferenda, mos Scripturae est, quae damnatum solet vocare damnandum. Inde est quod in Evangelio Dominus: Omnis - inquit - qui non crediderit in me, iam iudicatus est; quia non credidit in nomine unigeniti Filii Dei [n184] . Non quod infidelitas Christum negans, ante tempus iudicii, supplicio iuncta esset perpetuo; cum omnes qui ad fidem veniunt, prius fuerint infideles; sed ut censura praecipientis appareat, dicuntur peccata iam esse supplicia. Denique Adam ipsum, et ille liber qui Sapientia dicitur, et multorum opinio, secuta emendatione asserit expiatum.
pass_a_gloss: I will not indeed attack those who assert that Adam, if he had existed hearing the word, could have been transferred to immortality for remuneration. For we read Enoch and Elijah transferred, lest they see death. But other things are the institutions of nature, other the rewards of obedience. For the desert of one is not of so much, that it disturbs all things which were naturally instituted. Inborn mortality therefore would have exercised itself in the rest, even if that first had migrated from long duration into eternity. The matter is held not by an undeniable conjecture, but by a sure example, since indeed Enoch's sons could not be asserted from the condition of dying by the immortality of the parent. Nor let that perhaps be thought to meet, that if not sinners, yet all the just would escape to immortality without an intercession of bodily dissipation: since indeed Abel the first of the just, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the bands of the holy, both in the New and in the Old Testament, taught both their desert by virtues, and nature by death. The authority of Christ also confirmed a matter placed in the absolute. For when the Sadducees had brought a question to him by the example of a seven-married woman, asking, if an excitation of bodies were believed, by which husband she would most of all have to be claimed, he replied: You err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God; for in the resurrection they will neither marry, nor receive wives; for they will not even die. Conscious of his work, he expressed on account of what he had instituted marriages, namely that offspring would supply the losses of death; but immediately a munificent fertility would go having ceased, when greedy death has ceased. If therefore, Christ being witness who founded, fertility was created on account of this, that it would conflict with fragility, and this condition of marriages was ordained before sin; it appears also that mortality does not look to prevarication, but to nature to which marriages also are read to look. That law therefore which was promulgated, that is: On whatever day you eat from the interdict, by death you will die; a penal death is understood, not a corporal; hanging over sins, not seeds; which prevarication does not incur except, emendation does not escape except. But on the day of sin which is said to be about to be inflicted, it is a custom of Scripture, which is accustomed to call condemned him who must be condemned. From there it is that in the Gospel the Lord: Everyone, he says, who has not believed in me, has already been judged; because he did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. Not that infidelity denying Christ, before the time of judgment, was joined to a perpetual punishment; when all who come to faith were first unfaithful; but that the censure of the one precepting may appear, sins are said already to be punishments. Finally Adam himself, both that book which is called Wisdom, and the opinion of many, asserts expiated by a following emendation.

pass_b_english: I certainly will not attack those who think Adam, had he obeyed, could have been transferred to immortality as a reward. We read that Enoch and Elijah were taken away so as not to see death (Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5; 2 Kings 2:11). But nature’s arrangements are one thing, rewards for obedience another. One person’s merit is not so great as to overturn everything established naturally. Inborn mortality would therefore have continued operating in the rest, even if that first human had passed from prolonged life to eternity.

This rests not on a conjecture open to denial but on a certain example: Enoch’s children could not be freed from the condition of dying by their father’s immortality. Nor should anyone perhaps object that, if not sinners, at least all the righteous would have reached immortality without intervening bodily dissolution. Abel, first among the righteous, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and every company of saints in both Testaments displayed their merit through virtues and their nature through death.

Christ’s authority also confirmed this settled matter. The Sadducees put a question to him using a woman married seven times, asking which husband would chiefly claim her if bodily resurrection were believed. He answered: ‘You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor God’s power. In the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives, for they will not die’ (Matthew 22:29–30; Luke 20:35–36). Knowing his own work, he explained why he had instituted marriage: reproduction would make up death’s losses. Generous fertility would cease at once when grasping death ceased.

If, then, Christ who created it testifies that fertility was made to contend with frailty, and marriage’s condition was arranged before sin, mortality too plainly belongs not to transgression but to nature, to which we read marriage also belongs. The law promulgated—‘On the day you eat what is forbidden, you shall surely die’ (Genesis 2:17)—therefore means penal death, not bodily death. It threatens sins, not reproductive seed; only transgression incurs it, and only reform escapes it.

Its being said to fall on the day of sin follows Scripture’s practice of calling condemned someone still to be condemned. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who has not believed in me is already judged, because he has not believed in the name of God’s only-begotten Son’ (John 3:18). This does not mean that unbelief denying Christ was already joined to eternal punishment before the time of judgment, since everyone who comes to faith was formerly an unbeliever. Rather, to display the lawgiver’s judgment, sins are spoken of as already punishments. Finally, both the book called Wisdom and many people’s opinion affirm that Adam himself was cleansed through subsequent reform (Wisdom 10:1–2).
